# Introduction

The aim of this notebook is to use MaxEnt to estimate how climate change will impact the habitat of *Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila* for use in an ECBA submission.

The specific criteria being addressed is:

> *2b) **Continuing decline** observed, estimated, inferred or **projected** in any of: (i) extent of occurrence; (ii) area of occupancy; **(iii) area, extent and/or quality of habitat;** (iv) number of locations or subpopulations; (v) number of mature individuals."*

That is, we're trying to quantify the decline in the area of *niphophila* habitat under future climate change projections.

# Part 1: Data preparation

## Prepare observational data

### Download the occurrence data

The first thing I'll do is import the *E. niphophila* observational data. I'm using the `galah` package, which lets me access all of the data compiled by the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA). Observations come from a number of sources such as government agencies (mostly DEECCEW), herbaria, and iNaturalist.

Before downloading, I'm applying the built in data quality filter for species distribution modelling which accounts for outliers, duplicates, and invalid coordiantes. I'm also only downloading observations which are from Australia and which have lat/lon coordinates.

- [Descriptions of the data quality variables](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki)

- [Descriptions of the environmental variables](https://biocache.ala.org.au/fields?filter=name%3Ael%5B0-9%5D*&max=100&order=DESC&sort=classs)

```{r}
# If niph_raw has already been downloaded, import it. Otherwise, download observations from
# the Atlas of Living Australia, including >100 metadata columns.

# Note that this data will change as new records are uploaded.

niph_raw_path <- here::here("data/galah/niph_raw.rds")

if (file.exists(niph_raw_path)) {
  
  niph_raw <- readr::read_rds(niph_raw_path)
  
} else {
  
  # Construct an API call to galah. Some columns can be accessed in predefined groups
  
  niph_raw_call <- galah_call() |>
    identify("Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila") |>
    apply_profile(CSDM) |> 
    filter(
      occurrenceStatus == "PRESENT",
      !is.na(decimalLongitude),
      !is.na(decimalLatitude),
      country == "Australia"
      ) |>
    select(
      group = c(
        "basic", # record_id, lat/lon, etc.
        "event", # columns describing the observation process
        "assertions" # data quality checks
      ),
      starts_with("el"), # environmental variables
      "coordinateUncertaintyInMeters",
      "spatiallyValid",
      "isDuplicateOf",
      "outlierLayerCount",
      "year",
      "country",
      "stateProvince",
      "identifiedBy",
      "locality",
      "institutionCode"
    )
  
  # Download our occurrence data
  
  niph_raw <- atlas_occurrences(niph_raw_call, mint_doi = TRUE)
  
  # Save the raw data as an rds file
  
  readr::write_rds(niph_raw, niph_raw_path)
}

cat("Number of unfiltered Niphophila observations: ", nrow(niph_raw))
```

### Exclude low-quality data

Not all of this data is super high quality, so we can apply some data quality filters to try and filter out unreliable records:

- Records from before 1970

- Observations where the coordinate uncertainty is \> 1 km, or missing

```{r}
# Define a helper function to flag excluded records
# NA results to the condition are also flagged

flag <- function(df, condition, reason) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      exclusion_reason = coalesce(
        exclusion_reason, 
        if_else({{ condition }}, reason, NA, missing = reason)
      ),
      excluded = !is.na(exclusion_reason)
    )
}

#alps_states <- c("Victoria", "Australian Capital Territory", "New South Wales")

niph <- niph_raw |> 
  
  # Create an empty column to keep track of exclusions
  
  mutate(excluded = FALSE, exclusion_reason = NA_character_) |> 
  
  # Exclude and flag low-quality data
  
  #flag(occurrenceStatus != "PRESENT", "not present") |> 
  #flag(is.na(decimalLongitude) | is.na(decimalLatitude), "missing coordinates") |> 
  #flag(spatiallyValid == FALSE, "not spatially valid (ALA)") |> 
  #flag(!is.na(isDuplicateOf), "duplicate record (ALA)") |> 
  #flag(outlierLayerCount != 0, "outlier (ALA)") |> 
  #flag(country != "Australia", "not in Australia") |> 
  #flag(!(stateProvince %in% alps_states), "not in Alps states") |> 
  flag(is.na(year), "year missing") |> 
  flag(year < 1970, "pre-1970") |> 
  flag(is.na(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters), "coordinate uncertainty missing") |> 
  flag(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters > 1000, "coordinate uncertainty > 1 km") |> 
  
  # Select a more usable subset of columns
  
  select(
    recordID,
    scientificName,
    decimalLongitude,
    decimalLatitude,
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters,
    eventDate,
    year,
    basisOfRecord,
    identifiedBy,
    locality,
    stateProvince,
    dataResourceName,
    institutionCode, 
    excluded, 
    exclusion_reason
  ) |> 
  
  # Convert to a simple features object, i.e. explicitly spatial
  
  st_as_sf(coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"), crs = crs_geog)

# Tabulate the reasons for record removal

niph |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  count(exclusion_reason) |> 
  print()
```

We can view the observations we have left interactively.

```{r}
# View the records in an interactive map

mapview(niph |> filter(!excluded))
```

### Targeted outlier removal

Some observations are still suspicious, despite passing the data quality checks. I'll remove these records manually.

- One observation in Grampians NP which is outside the known range

- Two observations in Baw Baw which are from 1994 and are likely to be misidentifications of the Baw Baw subspecies (which was only described in 1994).

```{r}
# Identify suspicous records

targeted_exclusion <- c(
    "2c4dd780-74ef-4337-893b-250e47aa64a8" = "In Grampians NP, outside known range",
    "f1047be9-66f7-4ba6-9157-d0f1d906fa12" = "In Baw Baw, likely different subspecies",
    "56c4cb9d-db98-4f0c-8080-d75a281a5b06" = "In Baw Baw, likely different subspecies"
  ) |>
  tibble::enframe(name = "recordID", value = "reason")

# Flag these observations for exclusion

niph <- niph |> 
  flag(recordID %in% targeted_exclusion$recordID, "targeted exclusion")

niph |> 
  mutate(targeted_exclusion = exclusion_reason %in% "targeted exclusion") |> 
  filter(!excluded | targeted_exclusion) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "targeted_exclusion")
```

### Check the elevations

*E. niphophila* is known to inhabit altitudes above 1600 m (expert advice). To allow for some natural variation we'll allow records down to 1400 m, but any records below this altitude will be removed as they have a higher likelihood of being misidentifications.

```{r}
# Download a 5 degree tile of 3s elevation data which covers the observations.
# 3s data is on a grid of around 90 m x 90 m, which is more accurate than most of our data.

elev_3s <- geodata::elevation_3s(lon = 147.5, lat = -37.5, path = here::here("data"))

# Extract the elevation at each point

niph_elevs <- extract(elev_3s, vect(niph))

# Construct a buffer around each observation to account for positional uncertainty

niph_buffers <- buffer(
  vect(niph), 
  width = coalesce(niph$coordinateUncertaintyInMeters, 1)
)

# Extract the maximum and minimum elevations in each buffer zone

niph_elev_min <- extract(elev_3s, niph_buffers, fun = min, na.rm = TRUE)
niph_elev_max <- extract(elev_3s, niph_buffers, fun = max, na.rm = TRUE)

# Join the extracted elevation data back to our raw data set

niph <- niph |>
  mutate(
    elevation_m = niph_elevs[[2]],
    elevation_m_min = if_else(is.na(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters), NA, niph_elev_min[[2]]),
    elevation_m_max = if_else(is.na(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters), NA, niph_elev_max[[2]]),
    .after = coordinateUncertaintyInMeters
  )

# Flag records below the elevation threshold

niph <- niph |>
  flag(is.na(elevation_m), "elevation missing") |> 
  flag(elevation_m < 1400, "below elevation")

# Have a look at the observations we just filtered out

niph |> 
  mutate(below_elevation = exclusion_reason %in% "below elevation") |> 
  filter(!excluded | below_elevation) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "below_elevation", alpha.regions = 0.8)
```

I extracted the minimum and maximum elevation within the radius of coordinate uncertainty for each point. Debatably we could filter our observations based on the maximum possible elevation within this radius. However I ultimately decided to filter based on the elevation at the point, as the 1400 m threshold is likely to be generous already.

### Australian Alps bioregion

The Australian Alps bioregion will form the foundation of our study area definition. I'll also use it to exclude any final records which might not be where we expect to find *E. niphophila*.

```{r}
# The bioregions geodatabase doesn't download automatically. If needed, download it from
# https://fed.dcceew.gov.au/datasets/interim-biogeographic-regionalisation-for-australia-ibra-version-7-1-regions/about

# Import the Australian Alps bioregion polygon

aus_alps <- st_read(here::here("data/IBRA7_regions.gdb")) |>
  filter(REG_NAME_7 == "Australian Alps") |> 
  st_transform(crs_geog) |> 
  st_union()

# Identify any observations outside the bioregion

niph_outside_aus_alps <- niph |> 
  filter(!excluded) |> 
  st_filter(aus_alps, .predicate = st_disjoint)

# Plot just the points outside the bioregion

mapview(aus_alps, alpha.regions = 0.5, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph_outside_aus_alps, col.regions = "red")
```

There are three observations outside the bioregion, all clustered around Thredbo and all very close to the region. Let's look see exactly how far they are from the bioregon.

```{r}
niph_outside_aus_alps |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(dist_to_bioregion = st_distance(niph_outside_aus_alps, aus_alps)[, 1]) |> 
  select(
    dist_to_bioregion,
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters, 
    elevation_m,
    elevation_m_min,
    elevation_m_max
  )
```

Okay, so they're all within 100 m of the bioregion, which is within the bounds of their positional uncertainty. As there is also some inaccuracy in the bioregion definition I'm inclined to keep them in the data set.

## Define the study area

The study area is the region of environmental conditions we're interesting in contrasting our presence values against, i.e. places *Niphophila* could have reached and been recorded. We also need to include area beyond this range to give the model something to compare against.

I'll be basing the study area on the Australian Alps bioregion. All of our observations are within or very close to this area, however some parts of the bioregion have no observations and so either haven't been surveyed or aren't candidates for dispersal. As such, I'll remove any polygons which don't have an observation within 1 km.

```{r}
# To look at distances between points we need to move to a projected CRS

niph_proj <- niph |>
  filter(!excluded) |> 
  st_transform(crs_proj)

# Keep polygons within 1000 m of an observation

aus_alps_parts <- aus_alps |>
  st_transform(crs_proj) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  st_sf(geometry = _) |>
  mutate(keep = lengths(st_is_within_distance(geometry, niph_proj, dist = 1000)) > 0)

mapview(aus_alps_parts, zcol = "keep") +
  mapview(niph_proj, col.regions = "red")
```

In the above map the purple regions will be removed from the study area. This includes large areas around Baw Baw, Lake Mountain, and Mount Skene. These areas are well frequented, so *E. Niphophila* would have very likely been observed if it grew in these regions. The polygons removed further north tend to be small and peripheral or lower altitude.

To finish creating the study area I'll add a small buffer around the remaining polygons. This accounts for uncertainty in the bioregion definition.

```{r}
# Create a buffer around the study area. Also remove any small holes and smooth
# out the edges

study_area <- aus_alps_parts |> 
  filter(keep) |> 
  st_union() |> 
  st_buffer(dist = 100, joinStyle = "MITRE", mitreLimit = 2) |> 
  smoothr::fill_holes(units::set_units(1, km^2)) |> 
  smoothr::smooth(method = "ksmooth", smoothness = 2) |> 
  st_transform(crs_geog) |> 
  st_make_valid()

mapview(study_area, alpha.regions = 0.3, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(filter(niph, !excluded), col.regions = "red")
```

There are still parts of the study area which don't have any observations. Possibly these should be removed. Alternatively, multiple different study areas can be tested to see if it effects the output.

```{r}
# Double check that all observations are within the study area (expect 0 rows)

niph |> 
  filter(!excluded) |> 
  st_filter(study_area, .predicate = st_disjoint) |> 
  nrow()
```

Let's have a look at the elevation distribution in our study area.

```{r}
study_area_elev <- elev_3s |>
  crop(vect(study_area)) |>
  mask(vect(study_area))

plot(study_area_elev)
```

```{r}
hist(study_area_elev, breaks = 50, maxcell = ncell(study_area_elev))
```

A decent portion of our study area is below the 1400 m elevation threshold. This is good as it gives us information on non-habitat.

## Prepare current climate data

### Download current climate data

We can download gridded climate data from [WorldClim](https://www.worldclim.org/) at 30 second resolution (\~1 km² grid cells). This data has been averaged over the period 1970-2000 and is pretty standard to use in this sort of analysis.

```{r}
# WorldClim climate data is stored as 30x30 degree tiles. 
# Luckily, we only need one tile to cover the study area

clim_tile <- geodata::worldclim_tile(
  var = "bio",
  res = "0.5", # 0.5 minute resolution
  lon = 135,
  lat = -45,
  path = here::here("data")
)

# Crop the climate data to our study area, making sure that any grid cell 
# that touches the study area is included

clim_all <- clim_tile |>
  crop(vect(study_area), snap = "out") |>
  mask(vect(study_area), touches = TRUE)

# Create a key for interpreting the layer names

bio_names <- c(
  bio_1  = "Annual mean temp (°C)",
  bio_2  = "Mean diurnal range (°C)",
  bio_3  = "Isothermality (%)",
  bio_4  = "Temp seasonality (SD × 100)",
  bio_5  = "Max temp warmest month (°C)",
  bio_6  = "Min temp coldest month (°C)",
  bio_7  = "Temp annual range (°C)",
  bio_8  = "Mean temp wettest quarter (°C)",
  bio_9  = "Mean temp driest quarter (°C)",
  bio_10 = "Mean temp warmest quarter (°C)",
  bio_11 = "Mean temp coldest quarter (°C)",
  bio_12 = "Annual precipitation (mm)",
  bio_13 = "Precip wettest month (mm)",
  bio_14 = "Precip driest month (mm)",
  bio_15 = "Precip seasonality (CV)",
  bio_16 = "Precip wettest quarter (mm)",
  bio_17 = "Precip driest quarter (mm)",
  bio_18 = "Precip warmest quarter (mm)",
  bio_19 = "Precip coldest quarter (mm)"
)

# Plot a selection of environmental variables

plot_vars <- c("bio_1", "bio_2", "bio_5", "bio_6", "bio_7", "bio_12")

plot(clim_all[[plot_vars]], main = bio_names[plot_vars])
```

### Predictor selection

Many of these environmental variables are highly co-linear (they are all derived from monthly precipitation and temperature), and including all of them can cause model instability and make it difficult to assess the actual importance of each variable.

We can see this if we create a correlation plot.

```{r}
clim_corr <- layerCor(clim_all, "pearson", na.rm = TRUE)$correlation

corrplot::corrplot(
  clim_corr,
  method = "circle", 
  type = "upper",
  tl.col = "black"
)
```

To deal with this, we can refine our variables down into a more meaningful set of predictors.

The four 'interactive' variables (bio_8, bio_9, bio_18, bio_19) combine information about both temperature and precipitation, and are known to have non-physical discontinuities due to variation in which quarter is wettest or warmest. These are easy candidates for removal.

To narrow down the rest of the variables we can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF):

1.  Regress each variable against all other variables and get an $R^2$ which is a measure of the variable's variation that can't be explained by other variables.
2.  Calculate $VIF = 1 / (1-R^2)$.
3.  If the highest VIF is above a threshold (e.g 10) remove that variable.
4.  Recalculate the VIF for the remaining variables (which will have changed).
5.  Repeat until every VIF is below the threshold.

In practice this is implemented by `usdm::vifstep`.

```{r}
# First, remove the interactive variables

interactive_vars <- c("bio_8", "bio_9", "bio_18", "bio_19")

clim_candidates <- clim_all[[setdiff(names(clim_all), interactive_vars)]]

# Then do the VIF analysis

vif_threshold <- 10

vif_exclusions <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = vif_threshold) 

vif_exclusions
```

Using the VIF analysis we've lost bio_6, minimum temperature of the coldest month. It's probably accounted for by bio_1, bio_3, and bio_4 however I kind of want bio_6 in as it captures things like frost and snow. The correlation between bio_14 and bio_1 is also higher than I'd like (-0.87)

So, I'll run the VIF analysis again this time forcing bio_6 to be included.

```{r}
vif_exclusions2 <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = vif_threshold, keep = "bio_6") 

vif_exclusions2
```

In this set bio_6 (minimum temperature of the coldest month) has been exchanged for bio_1 (annual mean temperature). The maximum correlation between any two variables has also been reduced, though at -0.72 it's still quite high.

```{r}
clim <- usdm::exclude(clim_candidates, vif_exclusions2)

clim_vars <- names(clim)

plot(clim, main = bio_names[clim_vars])
```

### Environmental similarity analysis

Let's see how the landscape varies with respect to the areas around our occurrence points. To do this we can construct a Multivariate Environmental Similarity Surface (MESS). This involves calculating a similarity score for each variable and each cell when compared with our observations. The MESS value is the most dissimilar score across all variables.

```{r}
# We'll do the MESS analysis using our selected variables

mess_area <- crop(clim_tile[[clim_vars]], ext(145.5, 152, -38, -35))

# Extract the climatic variables at each observation

occs_z <- extract(mess_area, vect(filter(niph, !excluded)), ID = FALSE) |>
  drop_na()

# Get the MESS values across the full tile (not just the study area)

occs_mess <- predicts::mess(mess_area, occs_z, full = TRUE)

# Construct a MESS plot, overlayed with our study area

plot(occs_mess[["mess"]], col = hcl.colors(100, "RdBu"), main = "Environmental similarity")
plot(vect(study_area), border = "black", lwd = 1, add = TRUE)
```

And another version where the similarity has been binned so it's a bit easier to interpret.

```{r}
# Define breaks and colours

breaks <- c(-Inf, -50, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 50, 100)
colours <- hcl.colors(length(breaks) - 1, "RdBu")

plot(occs_mess[["mess"]], breaks = breaks, col = colours, main = "Environmental similarity")
plot(vect(study_area), border = "black", lwd = 1, add = TRUE)
```

Okay, looking pretty good then. Our study area captures all of the core habitat areas and there aren't any areas with a highly similar environment outside of our study area. There are some large chunks of our study area that have close to zero similarity, however there's not much that's actually dissimilar.

Let's actually calculate how much of the study area is dissimilar.

```{r}
# Extract the MESS values in the study area

study_area_mess <- mask(crop(occs_mess, vect(study_area)), vect(study_area))

# Find the proporation of negative MESS values

100 * global(study_area_mess[["mess"]] < 0, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
```

Almost 50% of our study area is dissimilar to our observations.

We can also see which variables are driving the dissimilarity.

```{r}
# Find the index of the most dissimilar variable in each cell

most_dissimilar <- which.min(occs_mess[[paste0(clim_vars, "_mess")]])
levels(most_dissimilar) <- data.frame(id = seq_along(clim_vars), var = clim_vars)

# Mask cells which are already similar

most_dissimilar_masked <- mask(most_dissimilar, occs_mess[["mess"]] < 0, maskvalues = FALSE)

# Plot

plot(most_dissimilar_masked, 
     col = hcl.colors(length(clim_vars), "Set 2"),
     main = "Most dissimilar variable (MESS < 0)")
plot(vect(study_area), add = TRUE, lwd = .5)
```

Interestingly, different variables drive dissimilarity in different areas. bio_15 is the only variable that isn't showing up much in this map and might be a candidate for removal.

```{r}
plot(occs_mess, col = colours, breaks = breaks)
```

Bio_15 is basically always positive, so may not have much predictive power. This tracks with it rarely being the most dissimilar variable.

## Thinning observational data

Our observations are biased towards where people look (i.e. along roads) rather than how *Niphophila* are actually distributed. Some observations are also clustered closely together, and if we included all of them certain environments would be overrepresented.

The standard way to get reduce these biases is through the process of observational thinning, whereby records which are close in geographic or environmental space are removed from the modelling data.

Note that not everyone is a fan of this process, e.g.

- Ten Caten, Cleber, and Tad Dallas. 2023. ‘Thinning Occurrence Points Does Not Improve Species Distribution Model Performance’. *Ecosphere* 14(12):e4703. doi:[10.1002/ecs2.4703](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.4703).

### Troubling transects

Before we can thin our whole data set, we need to deal with the 1999 transects in NSW. These observations are highly spatially correlated and may create a bias towards certain conditions. On the other hand, they are likely to be some of our best data in rarely-visited locations so we shouldn't throw them away completely.

```{r}
# Manually define boxes around the transect. These are only valid when observations 
# have also been filtered to 1999

transect_box_coords <- list(
  c(xmin = 148.33, ymin = -36.05, xmax = 148.39, ymax = -36.04),
  c(xmin = 148.45, ymin = -36.05, xmax = 148.49, ymax = -36.04),
  c(xmin = 148.33, ymin = -36.105, xmax = 148.49, ymax = -36.09),
  c(xmin = 148.28, ymin = -36.25, xmax = 148.49, ymax = -36.24)
)

transect_boxes <- transect_box_coords |>
  map(\(b) st_as_sfc(st_bbox(b, crs = st_crs(crs_geog)))) |> 
  do.call(what = c)

# Identify the transect records

niph_transects <- niph |> 
  filter(!excluded) |> 
  filter(year == 1999, stateProvince == "New South Wales") |> 
  st_filter(transect_boxes) |> 
  pull(recordID)

# Flag transect records

niph <- niph |> 
  mutate(transect = recordID %in% niph_transects)

# Visually confirm that everything is working

niph |> 
  mapview(zcol = "transect") +
  mapview(transect_boxes, col.regions = "red")
```

If you zoom into the transect boxes layer you can see that they constrain the transect observations correctly. There's one extra observation in one of the boxes, however it's from 2017 and has been excluded correctly.

Now we have to thin out the transect data. I'm going to do this using environmental thinning which splits each predictor into bins and then keeps a record whenever the transect reaches a new combination of conditions.

First, let's see how many grid cells there are along our transects.

```{r}
length(unique(cells(clim[[1]], vect(filter(niph, transect)))[, "cell"]))
```

Okay, so at most we will be keeping 45 transect observations (observations within the same grid cell are the same for our purposes).

Now let's do the environmental thinning.

```{r}
# Choose the number of bins to group the climate variables. 
# I tested a few values and the results are stable between 9-12 bins.

n_bins <- 10

# Find the range of each variable across the whole study area

ranges <- global(clim, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)

# Find the bin edges for each variable

bin_edges <- clim_vars |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(v) seq(ranges[v, "min"], ranges[v, "max"], length.out = n_bins + 1))

# Extract the values of each variable at our transect points

transect_clim <- niph |>
  filter(!excluded) |> 
  filter(transect)

transect_clim <- transect_clim |> 
  bind_cols(terra::extract(clim, vect(transect_clim), ID = FALSE))

# Define a function to assign each value to a bin number

assign_bin <- function(x, edges) {
  cut(x, breaks = edges, include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
}

# Keep one record per occupied combination of bins

niph_transect_thinned <- transect_clim |>
  mutate(across(all_of(clim_vars),
                \(x) assign_bin(x, bin_edges[[cur_column()]]),
                .names = "{.col}_bin")) |>
  group_by(across(ends_with("_bin"))) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |> 
  pull(recordID)

# Flag the thinned out records

niph <- niph |> 
  flag(transect & !(recordID %in% niph_transect_thinned), "transect thinning")
 
cat(length(niph_transect_thinned), "/", length(niph_transects), "transect observations kept")
```

We can also visualise the points which have been retained.

```{r}
niph |>
  filter(transect) |> 
  mutate(status = if_else(recordID %in% niph_transect_thinned, "kept", "removed")) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "status", alpha.regions = 1)
```

### Spatial thinning

Next we'll do spatial thinning across the whole data set, including the transects.

I originally did this using the `spThin` package which basically removes records one by one until no two are closer than a chosen distance, e.g. 1 km. By doing this randomly many times over we can choose the version that allows us to the keep the most data points. However, this process doesn't necessarily guarantee that we'll only have one observation per grid cell.

An alternative method is simpler. Group the observations by grid cell and keep the observation which has the lowest coordinate uncertainty. Recency is used as a tiebreaker.

```{r}
# Find the clmate grid cell of each record

niph$cell <- cells(clim[[1]], vect(niph))[, "cell"]

# Keep the most precise (then most recent) record in each cell

kept <- niph |>
  filter(!excluded) |>
  arrange(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters, desc(year)) |>
  distinct(cell, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  pull(recordID)

# Flag the excluded records

niph <- niph |>
  flag(!recordID %in% kept, "grid cell thinning")

cat(length(kept), "observations kept")
```

And let's see what we removed.

```{r}
niph |> 
  mutate(removed = exclusion_reason %in% "grid cell thinning") |> 
  filter(!excluded | removed) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "removed")
```

The majority of records which were removed are clustered around high-traffic areas like Hotham Heights or Charlotte Pass. This is what we wanted as these areas are overrepresented in our observation data. It should be noted that no environmental data was actually lost in this step - the model would only use one observation per grid cell anyway.

We could consider doing another round of thinning based on the actual distances between observations using `spThin`. This would further reduce the sampling bias, however it would also risk losing environmental data. I'll leave it here for now.

Before we move on to the modelling, it's also interesting to see why points were excluded.

```{r}
niph |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  count(exclusion_reason) |> 
  print()
```

# Part 2: Model fitting

## Training and testing data

### Background

Thinning partially accounts for bias in our observations, however they're still likely to be clustered around roads and other popular locations.

To the MaxEnt model, *presences* = *where the species lives* x *where people look*. If we sample the study area uniformly the model assumes that the presences just represent the habitat generally, and the output will show that the ideal habitat is most similar to the most sampled areas, i.e. around Kosciuszko.

To deal with this, we can create an approximate model of where people observe plants across our study area by looking at observation 'events' of all vascular plants. An event here is a unique combination of date and data resource in a specific grid cell.

```{r}
# Define a simplified polygon to use for requesting plant observations.
# The study area is buffered to ensure that areas are not cut-off by the simplification.

study_area_query <- study_area |>
  st_transform(crs_proj) |>
  st_buffer(5000) |>
  st_simplify(dTolerance = 2000) |>
  st_transform(crs_geog)

# Download the observations (or import cached copy)

plantae_raw_path <- here::here("data/galah/plantae_raw.rds")

if (file.exists(plantae_raw_path)) {
  
  plantae_raw <- readr::read_rds(plantae_raw_path)
  
} else {
  
  # Define a galah query which extracts all plant records in study_area_query.
  # Data quality filters are applied before downloading the data

  plantae_raw_call <- galah_call() |>
    identify("Plantae") |>
    apply_profile(CSDM) |> 
    filter(
      !is.na(decimalLongitude),
      !is.na(decimalLatitude),
      year >= 1970,
      coordinateUncertaintyInMeters <= 1000
    ) |>
    geolocate(study_area_query, type = "polygon")
  
  plantae_raw <- atlas_occurrences(plantae_raw_call, mint_doi = TRUE)
  readr::write_rds(plantae_raw, plantae_raw_path)
}

# Convert to a spatial object and reproject onto a projected crs

plantae <- plantae_raw |> 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"), crs = crs_geog) |>
  st_filter(study_area_query) |> 
  st_transform(crs_proj)

# Create a template raster that defines our grid

template_proj <- rast(
  ext(vect(st_transform(study_area_query, crs_proj))),
  resolution = 1000,
  crs = paste0("EPSG:", crs_proj)
)

# Match each record to its template grid cell, then count the number of 'events' per cell.
# An 'event' is a unique combination of observation date and data resource name. 
# This deals with the situation where e.g. one person makes 100 observations in the same 
# area on a single day.

plantae_events <- plantae |> 
  mutate(
    cell = cells(template_proj, vect(plantae))[, "cell"],
    date = as.Date(eventDate)
  ) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(date)) |> 
  distinct(cell, date, dataResourceName) |>
  count(cell)

# Write the event counts into a raster

event_counts <- rast(template_proj, vals = 0)
event_counts[plantae_events$cell] <- plantae_events$n

# Define a matrix of smoothing weights (like a 2D bell curve) extending 3 x sigma from the
# centre cell

bias_sigma <- 2000 # i.e. 2 cells
bg_kernel <- focalMat(template_proj, d = bias_sigma, type = "Gauss")

# Smooth plant observation surface usng the kerneal and map it back onto the climate grid

bias <- event_counts |>
  focal(w = bg_kernel, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) |>
  project(clim[[1]], method = "bilinear") |>
  mask(clim[[1]])

# Define maximum and minimum values for the bias surface

bias_ceiling <- 100
bias_floor <- 1

# Normalise the bias surface so the maximum value is set by bias_ceiling

bias <- bias_ceiling * bias / global(bias, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]

# Also set a minimum value for areas with low bias values to ensure they are stills sampled

bias <- clamp(bias, lower = bias_floor, values = TRUE)

plot(bias, main = "Sampling effort")
```

It's a bit easier to see the details of this surface on a log scale. We can also adjust the raw values so that they're relative to the median sampling effort.

```{r}
bias_rel <- bias / global(bias, median, na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]

plot(log10(bias_rel),
     main = "Relative sampling effort (log10)",
     plg = list(
       at = log10(c(0.5, 1, 3, 10, 30)),
       labels = c("0.5×", "1×", "3×", "10×", "30×")
     ))
```

And again, but this time with the *E. niphophila* observations on top.

```{r}
plot(log10(bias_rel),
     main = "Relative sampling effort (log10)",
     plg = list(
       at = log10(c(0.5, 1, 3, 10, 30)),
       labels = c("0.5×", "1×", "3×", "10×", "30×")
     ))
points(vect(filter(niph, !excluded)), cex = 0.2, col = "red")
```

Okay, so we can see that a lot of our observations are clustered around the ski-resort hotspots. It's good to see that there are some highly visited areas with no observations and some observations in areas with few visitors. There is a danger of overcompensating here (as the areas around the ski resorts are the kind of habitat where we'd expect to see a lot of *niphophila*) however without an additional data source (e.g. satellite data) I think this is as good as I can do.

Now let's sample from this background. I'm a bit concerned this bias is overweighted, so I'm going to sample it based on an exponent, `bias^k`.

- If k = 0 it's a uniform background (no bias)

- If k = 1 it's the full background bias

- If k = 0.5 it's the square root of the bias surface, so a gentler bias correction

- And so on for intermediate values

```{r}
# Number of background points

n_bg <- 5000

# Define a function to scale the bias surface by an exponential factor, k

bias_k <- function(k) {
  bias_scaled <- bias_ceiling * (bias / global(bias, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])^k
  mask(bias_scaled, bias)
}

# We also need a function to sample points from the background for a given k value

bg_sample_k <- function(k, n_bg) {
  spatSample(
    bias_k(k), 
    size = n_bg,
    method = "weights", 
    xy = TRUE, 
    values = FALSE, 
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) |>
    as_tibble()
}

# Sample background points for different k values, weighted by the bias surface

k_vals <- c(0, 0.5, 1)

bg_samples <- k_vals |> 
  set_names(\(k) paste0("k_", k)) |> 
  map(\(k) bg_sample_k(k, n_bg))

# Plot each background sample for comparison

bg_samples |> 
  list_rbind(names_to = "sample") |> 
  mutate(sample = forcats::fct_inorder(sample)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = study_area) +
  geom_point(aes(x, y), size = 0.1, alpha = 0.3, colour = "darkgreen") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample) +
  theme_void()
```

Let's also check that these most biased background points still describe the full environmental range in the study area.

```{r}
# Extract the climate values at each background points

bg_bias_z <- extract(clim, as.matrix(bg_samples$k_1))

# Calculate the MESS of the study area compared to the background reference

bg_mess <- predicts::mess(clim, bg_bias_z)

# Plat areas with MESS < 0

plot(bg_mess < 0, main = "Outside background environmental range")
```

Yay, basically the whole study area is similar to the background points.

### Partitions

We have to partition our observations into training and testing data. This can't just be done randomly because of the spatial correlation in the environment — if the model is tested at grid cell right next to where it was trained then it's going to be able to predict habitat suitability by interpolating between training points rather than by actually describing the habitat accurately.

I'm partitioning the data into 4 folds. Each of these will be excluded one at a time and used to test a model based on data from the other three folds. There's a few ways we can do this, but the most straightforward are the block and checkerboard methods. I'm going to construct a few different partition sets using different parameters and see how they compare.

```{r}
# Block: This splits at the medians of latitude and longitude
# This is a baseline test, it's unlikely to be reliable given the shape of our study area

block <- list("Block" = ENMeval::get.block(occs, bg_uniform))

# Checkerboard: a checkerboard with each square then broken up into another checkerboard
# It makes sense if you see it.

# Vary the number of cells icluded in the smallest layer of the checkerboard

cb_factors <- c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25) # e.g. 5 x 5 cells, etc.
cb_factors <- set_names(cb_factors, paste0("Checkerboard (", cb_factors, ", 2)"))

# Create checkerboard partitions for each factor

get_checkerboard <- function(aggregation_factor) {
  ENMeval::get.checkerboard(
    occs = occs, 
    envs = clim, 
    bg = bg_uniform, 
    aggregation.factor = c(aggregation_factor, 2)
  )
}

# Combine the block and checkerboard partitions into a single list

partitions <- c(
  block,
  map(cb_factors, get_checkerboard)
)

# Map the partitions onto their corresponding background tiles

partition_tiles <- partitions |>
  imap(\(folds, name) mutate(bg_uniform, fold = factor(folds$bg.grp), method = name)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(method = forcats::fct_inorder(method))

# Plot each of the partition options

ggplot(partition_tiles, aes(x, y, fill = fold)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ method, ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(fill = "Fold") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

From visual comparison, it's pretty clear that the block partitioning won't be suitable - there will be large biases towards whichever partitions end up containing the hotspots around the various ski towns.

The checkerboard partitions are more difficult to choose between. Generally larger spatial blocks are going to be better because each fold ends up being more independent. On the other hand, if we go too big, then the folds are no longer representative of the environment. It's also important that each fold contains similar numbers of background and occurrence points.

Let's start by looking at how the points are distributed between the folds.

```{r}
# Extract the number of occurrences and background points in each fold

fold_sizes <- function(folds, name) {
  full_join(
    count(tibble(fold = folds$occs.grp), fold, name = "presences"),
    count(tibble(fold = folds$bg.grp), fold, name = "background"),
    by = "fold"
  )
}

fold_table <- imap(partitions, fold_sizes) |> 
  list_rbind(names_to = "method")

# Plot the proportion of points in each fold

fold_table |>
  pivot_longer(c(presences, background), names_to = "type", values_to = "n") |>
  group_by(method, type) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(method = forcats::fct_inorder(method)) |>
  ggplot(aes(method, prop, colour = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), size = 2.5, shape = 1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, 
       y = "Proportion of points in fold", 
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Fold balance by partition method"
      )
```

- A perfectly balanced partition would have all eight dots on the dashed line at 25%.

- The block partition splits the occurrences perfectly, however one partition contains significantly less background

- The background points are generally well balanced for all of the checkerboards, with smaller boxes generally having a more even distribution

- Occurrence points are less evenly distributed in the checkerboard, with some randomness depending on e.g. which fold ends up with the points around Kosciuszko. (10, 2) is least balanced, though the other options all perform similarly. (25, 2) is the most balanced.

The other criteria we have to consider is the environmental similarity of each fold. We can do this by calculating the environmental similarity of each fold to its three training folds (thankfully there are package functions to do this for me). Areas with negative values represent conditions unrepresented in the test fold.

```{r}
# Calculate the environmental similarity of each test fold to its training folds.

# Reformat climate variables at occurrence and background for ENMeval

occs_z <- occs |> 
  bind_cols(extract(clim, as.matrix(occs))) |> 
  rename(longitude = x, latitude = y)

bg_z <- bg_uniform |> 
  bind_cols(extract(clim, as.matrix(bg_uniform))) |> 
  rename(longitude = x, latitude = y)

# Calculate the environmental similarity for each grid cell

envsim_tbl <- imap(partitions, \(folds, name) {
  ENMeval::evalplot.envSim.hist(
    occs.z = occs_z,
    bg.z = bg_z,
    occs.grp = folds$occs.grp,
    bg.grp = folds$bg.grp,
    ref.data = "bg",
    return.tbl = TRUE
  )
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "method")

# Plot the proportion of negative MESS scores for each fold

envsim_tbl |> 
  filter(method != "Block") |> 
  mutate(method = forcats::fct_inorder(method)) |>
  group_by(method, partition) |> 
  summarise(prop_dissimilar = mean(mess < 0), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(method, prop_dissimilar, colour = partition)) +
  #geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), size = 2.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of points with MESS < 0", colour = "Partition",
       title = "Environmental similarity by partition method")
```

- Block values were excluded from this plot as they perform so much worse they're off the chart.

- The proportion of test points outside the training environment increases with square size, up to a maximum of around 10% for one of the (25, 2) folds.

With these findings in mind, I think checkerboard (20, 2) strikes the best balance between environmental similarity and balancing the pionts between folds. I'll also do a sensitivity analysis using (15, 2) and (25, 2) to see if our results change much - ideally the choice of partitioning method shouldn't matter much.

## Fit

```{r}
folds <- partitions[["Checkerboard (20, 2)"]]

enm <- ENMeval::ENMevaluate(
  occs = occs,
  envs = clim,
  bg = bg_uniform,
  algorithm = "maxnet",
  partitions = "user",
  user.grp = folds,
  tune.args = list(
    fc = c("L", "LQ", "LQH", "H"),
    rm = seq(0.5, 4, by = 0.5)
  ),
  parallel = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
results <- ENMeval::eval.results(enm)

ENMeval::evalplot.stats(
  enm,
  stats = c("or.10p", "auc.val"),
  x.var = "rm",
  color = "fc"
)
```

```{r}
best_cv <- results |>
  filter(or.10p.avg == min(or.10p.avg)) |>
  filter(auc.val.avg == max(auc.val.avg))

best_aicc <- results |>
  filter(delta.AICc == 0)

bind_rows(cv = best_cv, aicc = best_aicc, .id = "criterion") |>
  select(criterion, tune.args, auc.val.avg, or.10p.avg, delta.AICc, ncoef)
```

```{r}
best_args <- as.character(best_cv$tune.args)

best_model <- ENMeval::eval.models(enm)[[best_args]]

plot(best_model, type = "cloglog")    # response curves
current_pred <- ENMeval::eval.predictions(enm)[[best_args]]

plot(current_pred, main = "Current habitat suitability")
```

```{r}
plot(current_pred)
points(vect(filter(niph, !excluded)), pch = 20, cex = 0.4, col = "red")
```

```{r}
mapview(current_pred)



```

```{r}
niph_kept <- filter(niph, !excluded)
niph_kept$suitability <- extract(current_pred, vect(niph_kept), ID = FALSE)[[1]]


niph_kept |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(stateProvince) |>
  summarise(median_suitability = median(suitability), n = n()) |> 
  print()
```

```{r}
range_polys <- niph_kept |>
  st_transform(crs_proj) |>
  st_buffer(5000) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_cast("POLYGON")

niph_kept$range_id <- st_intersects(st_transform(niph_kept, crs_proj), range_polys) |>
  map_int(\(x) x[1])

niph_kept |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(range_id) |>
  summarise(median_suitability = median(suitability), n = n()) |>
  arrange(median_suitability) |> 
  print()
```

```{r}
mapview(niph_kept, zcol = "range_id")
```
